evidence.claim: The Indian Lakes drive links Topton and Almond by US 129 and NC 28.
evidence.quote: This byway also connects to the Indian Lakes Scenic Byway (at Topton and Almond via US 129 and North Carolina Highway 28, or NC 28).

evidence.claim: NC 28’s Almond–Deals Gap section is a state scenic byway.
evidence.quote: NC 28 overlaps with two state scenic byways: the Waterfall Byway, between Highlands and Franklin,  and the Indian Lake Scenic Byway, between Almond and Deals Gap.

evidence.claim: The North Carolina Department of Transportation describes the overlapping Fontana Byway as a winding drive along Cheoah Lake at the base of the Great Smoky Mountains, highlighting lake views and the engineering of Fontana Dam.
evidence.quote: Fontana Byway weaves in and out around the base of the Great Smoky Mountains along Cheoah Lake which is part of the Little Tennessee River.

evidence.claim: The Tennessee Valley Authority built Fontana Dam during World War II to meet electricity demand from the aluminum industry.
evidence.quote: which built the dam in the early 1940s to satisfy the skyrocketing electricity demands in the Tennessee Valley to support the aluminum industry at the height of World War II

evidence.claim: Its reservoir submerged most of NC 288, the highway between Deals Gap and Bryson City.
evidence.quote: The construction of Fontana Dam led to the flooding of most of North Carolina Highway 288, which connected Deals Gap and Bryson City.

evidence.claim: A surviving western section returned as NC 288 before new construction connected Fontana and Almond in 1954; the whole remaining NC 288 route then became NC 28.
evidence.quote: The second NC 288 was a return along the western part of the highway that wasn't submerged, linking to the relocated Fontana community.  In 1954, new construction was completed between Fontana and Almond, and all of NC 288 was renumbered NC 28.

evidence.claim: From Topton, US 129 heads north through Robbinsville toward Deals Gap.
evidence.quote: From the Georgia state line, it travels northeast to Topton, where it goes north to Robbinsville followed by Tennessee, through Deals Gap.

evidence.claim: The courthouse in the center of Robbinsville is the third to serve Graham County.
evidence.quote: The third and current building was completed in 1942.

evidence.claim: The original courthouse was built in 1874. Two decades later, its floor gave way while the building was packed for a murder trial.
evidence.quote: The first Graham County Courthouse was constructed in Robbinsville in 1874, but its floor collapsed two decades later while the building was packed during a murder trial.

evidence.claim: A replacement followed in 1895, the last wooden courthouse built in North Carolina.
evidence.quote: A replacement, built in 1895, was the last wooden courthouse built in North Carolina.

evidence.claim: The current building, completed in 1942, is a stone Classical Revival design by Barber and McMurry of Knoxville.
evidence.quote: The current courthouse is a Classical Revival structure designed by Barber and McMurry of Knoxville, Tennessee. It is fashioned from stone

evidence.claim: Works Progress Administration funding helped build it during the Depression era.
evidence.quote: The building is one of three North Carolina courthouses built with funds from the Depression-era Works Progress Administration.

evidence.claim: The T-shaped building stands at 12 North Main Street, in the center of the county seat.
evidence.quote: The T-shaped building occupies a prominent location in the center of Robbinsville.

evidence.claim: Deals Gap names both a mountain pass on the state line and a community 0.7 miles south of it, at US 129 and NC 28.
evidence.quote: Deals Gap (el. 1,988 ft (606 m)) is a mountain pass along the North Carolina–Tennessee state line, bordering the Great Smoky Mountains National Park and near the Little Tennessee River.  At 0.7 miles (1.1 km) south of the gap is the unincorporated community that shares the same name, located at the intersection of US 129 and NC 28.

evidence.claim: Across the line in Tennessee, US 129 becomes the eleven-mile Tail of the Dragon, a destination for motorcycle and sports-car drivers.
evidence.quote: The first 11 miles of US 129 in Tennessee, from Deals Gap on the North Carolina–Tennessee state line to the southern terminus of the Foothills Parkway, is known as The Tail of the Dragon from its winding course. It is a popular motorcycle and sports car destination.

evidence.claim: The two-lane road runs mostly through forest, with overlooks and places to pull off.
evidence.quote: It mostly travels through a forested area and there are a few scenic overlooks and pull-off points along the route.

evidence.claim: The Dragon name has been used since 1981.
evidence.quote: a stretch of two-lane road known since 1981 as "Tail of the Dragon"

evidence.claim: The Appalachian Trail crosses the top of Fontana Dam, 480 feet above its base.
evidence.quote: At 480 feet (150 m) high, Fontana is the tallest dam in the Eastern United States;

evidence.claim: The Tennessee Valley Authority began construction on January 1, 1942.
evidence.quote: construction of Fontana Dam began on January 1, 1942.

evidence.claim: Two generators began operating in January 1945, supplying electricity for wartime aluminum production.
evidence.quote: Two generating units were placed in operation on January 20, 1945, in time to provide crucial energy for aluminum production in the closing months of World War II.

evidence.claim: The reservoir required the relocation of 1,311 families, 1,047 graves and more than 60 miles of roads.
evidence.quote: Some 1,311 families, 1,047 graves, and more than 60 miles (97 km) of roads had to be relocated out of the project area.

evidence.claim: Fontana, Bushnell, Forney and Judson were completely submerged.
evidence.quote: The towns of Fontana, Bushnell, Forney, and Judson were completely inundated by the formation of Lake Fontana.

evidence.claim: The dam takes its name from the lost lumber and copper-mining town at Eagle Creek.
evidence.quote: Fontana is named for the now-inundated town of Fontana, a former lumber and copper-mining hub once located at the mouth of Eagle Creek.

evidence.claim: The Appalachian Trail crosses the top of Fontana Dam
evidence.quote: The Appalachian Trail crosses the top of the dam.

evidence.claim: Fontana Lake has coves and islands formed from former mountain peaks; when water levels fall, its steep banks are exposed.
evidence.quote: The lake has many inlets into coves and many islands formed from former mountain peaks, especially near the eastern end. As with most dam-impounded lakes, the steep banks are exposed when water levels are low.

evidence.claim: At Almond, the post office, school and railway depot were moved in 1943 during dam construction.
evidence.quote: During the construction of Fontana Dam, the post office, school, and railway depot located here were moved during 1943.

evidence.claim: The T-shaped building stands at 12 North Main Street, in the center of the county seat.
evidence.quote: The Graham County Courthouse is located at 12 North Main Street in Robbinsville, the county seat of Graham County, North Carolina.

evidence.quote: Fontana Village has been adapted and expanded as a summer resort; some of the original 1940s buildings still are used.
